title: Quaker silence
hookLine: Quakers gather in silence and speak only when moved, seeking "that of God in every one" (George Fox)
carry: that of god in every one

cards: Benches facing each other. No altar up front, no pulpit, nobody in robes. People come in, sit down, and say nothing.
A long quiet stretch goes by. A cough. A chair creaks.
Then a woman near the window stands up, says a few sentences about her father, and sits down again. Nobody replies. The silence closes back over, like water.

Then two people shake hands, everyone turns and shakes hands, and that's the service. This is a Quaker meeting for worship, the silent kind. Most of the prayer in these last days has been one person, alone.

teach.b: Quakers call themselves the Religious Society of Friends; you met their way of meeting on day nine hundred twenty-five.
Their founder, an Englishman named George Fox, wrote a letter to fellow ministers that carries today's line.
Live in a way that preaches without words, he urges, and then "you will come to walk cheerfully over the world, answering that of God in every one." First, why silence.
As Friends see it, if there is something of God in every person, nobody needs to stand in between. So in the silent kind of meeting there's no planned sermon and no appointed speaker.
Second, when someone speaks. Anyone may stand, a child, a visitor, a longtime member, if they feel moved to. Friends call this ministry.
It's meant to come out of the silence, not out of a prepared speech, and it's usually short. No one debates it afterward. The silence takes it back.
Third, that of God in every one. Notice Fox's word: answering. Not just finding something holy in other people, but responding to it.
Friends have read the phrase as a call to treat every person as someone who can hear God directly, which has shaped how they handle disagreement, decisions and conflict.
Fourth, not every meeting is silent.

teach.h: ANSWERING THAT OF GOD IN EVERY ONE.
teach.b: Some Quaker meetings have pastors, hymns and sermons; others, like the one in the hook, gather in silence. Both are Quaker. And the handshake?
It's simply how a silent meeting knows it's over.

how: In unprogrammed Quaker meetings, Friends gather in silence, anyone may stand to speak briefly when moved, and the meeting ends with handshakes; programmed Friends meetings include pastors, hymns and sermons.

games.q: you're sitting in a silent meeting and a thought rises that feels worth saying. what do Friends do?
o: prepare it carefully and give a speech.
stand only if moved, say it briefly, then sit.
wait for the minister to call on you.
games.why: there's no appointed speaker. ministry comes out of the silence, is usually short, and nobody argues with it afterward.

practice: If someone is near you right now, a partner, a roommate, a stranger on the bus, let your silence include them; if you're alone, bring a few people to mind and sit with them as if the bench were facing you.
Don't send them advice; just wait together, listening. If a word rises that feels worth saying, you can hold it, since not every word needs to be spoken.

wordCard.voice: Quaker silence. Friends waiting together without a planned sermon, speaking only when moved, trusting that something of God is in every one. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: that of God in every one. Answering it, not only finding it. I'll be here tomorrow.
